clinicalPearls: Rare X-linked motor neurone disorder of infancy caused by variants in UBA1, the gene encoding the ubiquitin-activating enzyme E1
Affects male infants, who present with profound hypotonia, weakness, areflexia and often multiple congenital contractures (arthrogryposis)
Distinct from the common SMN1-related spinal muscular atrophy and negative on standard SMN1 testing, so a separate genetic diagnosis is required
Bone fractures and dysmorphic features may accompany the neuromuscular presentation
Electrophysiology shows a motor neuronopathy pattern with denervation on needle examination and reduced motor amplitudes, while sensory studies are preserved
The disorder implicates disturbed protein degradation via the ubiquitin-proteasome system in anterior horn cell loss
Diagnosis requires UBA1 sequencing in a male infant with an SMA-like picture and a compatible X-linked family history
reference.pathophysiology: X-linked spinal muscular atrophy results from variants in UBA1, which encodes the ubiquitin-activating enzyme E1 that initiates the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway responsible for targeted protein degradation. Impaired activation of ubiquitin disrupts protein homeostasis in motor neurones, leading to degeneration of anterior horn cells and consequent denervation of skeletal muscle. Because the gene lies on the X chromosome, hemizygous males are affected while carrier females are typically unaffected. Loss of lower motor neurones produces the hypotonia, weakness and areflexia, and antenatal weakness contributes to the congenital contractures; sensory pathways are spared, giving a pure motor electrophysiological picture.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital myopathies and congenital myasthenic syndromes
Arthrogryposis multiplex congenita of other cause
Other rare non-5q spinal muscular atrophies
additionalInvestigations: SMN1 testing to exclude classic spinal muscular atrophy
UBA1 sequencing in male infants with an SMA-like phenotype
Nerve conduction studies and electromyography showing motor neuronopathy with preserved sensory responses
Skeletal survey for fractures and contractures
Pedigree analysis for an X-linked inheritance pattern
redFlags: Neonatal respiratory failure requiring urgent support
Feeding and swallowing difficulty with aspiration risk
Rapidly progressive weakness in early infancy
reference.prognosis: Generally severe, with significant early morbidity and frequently early respiratory compromise; outcome depends on the degree of weakness and respiratory involvement.
pitfalls: Stopping at a negative SMN1 result and not pursuing UBA1 in an affected male
Attributing arthrogryposis to a primary joint or muscle disorder alone
Overlooking the X-linked pattern in the family history
Missing associated fractures and dysmorphism as diagnostic clues
references: GeneReviews: UBA1-Related X-Linked Spinal Muscular Atrophy
Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Proactive respiratory support with non-invasive or invasive ventilation and secretion clearance for early respiratory compromise
Nutritional support and safe feeding, with nasogastric or gastrostomy feeding where swallowing is unsafe
Orthopaedic and physiotherapy management of arthrogryposis and contractures, with attention to fracture risk
Physiotherapy and careful positioning to preserve function and prevent complications of immobility
Multidisciplinary neuromuscular care coordinating neurology, respiratory, orthopaedics and rehabilitation
Anticipatory and palliative care planning given the frequently severe prognosis
Genetic counselling with UBA1 testing after exclusion of SMN1-related spinal muscular atrophy, and carrier testing of the mother
